claim: Open data allows researchers to explore pre-existing datasets in new ways.
source: Open data allows researchers to explore pre-existing datasets in new ways.
evidence: This is a general statement about open data capabilities presented in the abstract without specific supporting data in this manuscript.

claim: If many researchers reuse the same dataset, multiple statistical testing may increase false positives.
source: However, if many researchers reuse the same dataset, multiple statistical testing may increase false positives.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulations and empirical analyses presented in the manuscript showing increased false positive rates with sequential testing.

claim: Sequential hypothesis testing on the same dataset by multiple researchers can inflate error rates.
source: Here we demonstrate that sequential hypothesis testing on the same dataset by multiple researchers can inflate error rates.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulations showing probability of false positives increases with sequential tests (Figure 1A).

claim: There has been a push to make scientific datasets associated with published papers openly available to other researchers in recent years.
source: In recent years, there has been a push to make the scientific datasets associated with published papers openly available to other researchers (Nosek et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nosek et al., 2015.

claim: Making data open will allow other researchers to both reproduce published analyses and ask new questions of existing datasets.
source: Making data open will allow other researchers to both reproduce published analyses and ask new questions of existing datasets (Molloy, 2011; Pisani et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Molloy, 2011 and Pisani et al., 2016.

claim: The ability to explore pre-existing datasets in new ways should make research more efficient and has the potential to yield new discoveries.
source: The ability to explore pre-existing datasets in new ways should make research more efficient and has the potential to yield new discoveries (Weston et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weston et al., 2019.

claim: The availability of open datasets will increase over time as funders mandate and reward data sharing and other open research practices.
source: The availability of open datasets will increase over time as funders mandate and reward data sharing and other open research practices (McKiernan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to McKiernan et al., 2016.

claim: At present, researchers reusing datasets tend to correct for the number of statistical tests that they perform on the datasets.
source: At present, researchers reusing datasets tend to correct for the number of statistical tests that they perform on the datasets.
evidence: This is a statement about current research practice without specific supporting evidence in the manuscript.

claim: When performing hypothesis testing it is important to take into account all of the statistical tests that have been performed on the datasets.
source: However, as we discuss in this article, when performing hypothesis testing it is important to take into account all of the statistical tests that have been performed on the datasets.
evidence: This is the main argument of the paper, supported by simulations and empirical examples showing increased false positives without sequential correction.

claim: A distinction can be made between simultaneous and sequential correction procedures when correcting for multiple tests.
source: A distinction can be made between simultaneous and sequential correction procedures when correcting for multiple tests.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about statistical correction procedures.

claim: Simultaneous procedures correct for all tests at once, while sequential procedures correct for the latest in a non-simultaneous series of tests.
source: Simultaneous procedures correct for all tests at once, while sequential procedures correct for the latest in a non-simultaneous series of tests.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about statistical correction procedures.

claim: Sequential correction procedures are harder to implement than simultaneous procedures as they require keeping track of the total number of tests that have been performed by others.
source: Sequential correction procedures are harder to implement than simultaneous procedures as they require keeping track of the total number of tests that have been performed by others.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practical implementation challenges of sequential correction procedures.

claim: Obtaining all three desiderata (sharing incentive, open access, and stable false positive rate) is not possible.
source: We will show that obtaining all three of these desiderata is not possible.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of different correction procedures and their trade-offs (Table 1).

claim: The current practice of ignoring sequential tests leads to an increased false positive rate in the scientific literature.
source: We will demonstrate below that the current practice of ignoring sequential tests leads to an increased false positive rate in the scientific literature.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulations (Figure 1A) and empirical analysis (Figure 3) showing dramatic increases in false positives without sequential correction.

claim: Sequentially correcting for data reuse can reduce the number of false positives compared to current practice.
source: Further, we show that sequentially correcting for data reuse can reduce the number of false positives compared to current practice.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulations (Figure 1B-D) and empirical analysis (Figure 3) showing reduced false positives with sequential correction procedures.

claim: All the sequential correction proposals must compromise (to some degree) on one of the desiderata.
source: However, all the proposals considered here must still compromise (to some degree) on one of the above desiderata.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of each correction procedure's compatibility with the three desiderata (Table 1).

claim: fMRI BOLD activation was found in a dead salmon when appropriate corrections for multiple tests were not performed.
source: A famous example of the consequences of uncorrected multiple simultaneous statistical tests is the finding of fMRI BOLD activation in a dead salmon when appropriate corrections for multiple tests were not performed (Bennett et al., 2010; Bennett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett et al., 2010 and Bennett et al., 2009.

claim: A family is a set of tests which we relate the same error rate to (familywise error).
source: A family is a set of tests which we relate the same error rate to (familywise error).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about statistical families.

claim: What constitutes a family has been challenging to precisely define, and the existing guidelines often contain additional imprecise terminology.
source: What constitutes a family has been challenging to precisely define, and the existing guidelines often contain additional imprecise terminology (e.g. Cox, 1965; Games, 1971; Hancock and Klockars, 1996; Hochberg and Tamhane, 1987; Miller, 1981).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Cox, 1965; Games, 1971; Hancock and Klockars, 1996; Hochberg and Tamhane, 1987; Miller, 1981.

claim: Tests are considered part of a family when multiple variables are being tested with no predefined hypothesis (i.e. exploration or data-dredging).
source: Generally, tests are considered part of a family when: (i) multiple variables are being tested with no predefined hypothesis (i.e. exploration or data-dredging), or (ii) multiple pre-specified tests together help support the same or associated research questions (Hancock and Klockars, 1996; Hochberg and Tamhane, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hancock and Klockars, 1996 and Hochberg and Tamhane, 1987.

claim: Tests are considered part of a family when multiple pre-specified tests together help support the same or associated research questions.
source: Generally, tests are considered part of a family when: (i) multiple variables are being tested with no predefined hypothesis (i.e. exploration or data-dredging), or (ii) multiple pre-specified tests together help support the same or associated research questions (Hancock and Klockars, 1996; Hochberg and Tamhane, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hancock and Klockars, 1996 and Hochberg and Tamhane, 1987.

claim: There can be considerable disagreements about what constitutes a statistical family, which can include both very liberal and very conservative inclusion criteria.
source: Even if following these guidelines, there can still be considerable disagreements about what constituents a statistical family, which can include both very liberal and very conservative inclusion criteria.
evidence: This is supported by the example of factorial ANOVA where different researchers disagree on family definitions.

claim: Some have argued that the main effect and interaction in factorial ANOVA are separate families as they answer 'conceptually distinct questions'.
source: An example of this discrepancy is seen in using a factorial ANOVA. Some have argued that the main effect and interaction are separate families as they answer 'conceptually distinct questions' (e.g. page 291 of Maxwell and Delaney, 2004), while others would argue the opposite and state they are the same family (e.g. Cramer et al., 2016; Hancock and Klockars, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxwell and Delaney, 2004.

claim: Some have argued that the main effect and interaction in factorial ANOVA are the same family.
source: An example of this discrepancy is seen in using a factorial ANOVA. Some have argued that the main effect and interaction are separate families as they answer 'conceptually distinct questions' (e.g. page 291 of Maxwell and Delaney, 2004), while others would argue the opposite and state they are the same family (e.g. Cramer et al., 2016; Hancock and Klockars, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cramer et al., 2016 and Hancock and Klockars, 1996.

claim: Recommendations have directed researchers to define and justify their family of tests a priori.
source: Given the substantial leeway regarding the definition of family, recommendations have directed researchers to define and justify their family of tests a priori (Hancock and Klockars, 1996; Miller, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hancock and Klockars, 1996 and Miller, 1981.

claim: There has been considerable effort placed into clearly demarcating what is exploratory and what is confirmatory given issues regarding replication in recent years.
source: Given issues regarding replication in recent years (Open Science Collaboration, 2015), there has been considerable effort placed into clearly demarcating what is exploratory and what is confirmatory.
evidence: Supported by citation to Open Science Collaboration, 2015.

claim: One prominent definition is that confirmatory research requires preregistration before seeing the data.
source: One prominent definition is that confirmatory research requires preregistration before seeing the data (Wagenmakers et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wagenmakers et al., 2012.

claim: Current practice often involves releasing open data with the original research article.
source: However, current practice often involves releasing open data with the original research article.
evidence: This is a statement about current research practice.

claim: All data reuse may be guided by the original or subsequent analyses (a HARKing-like problem where methods are formulated after some results are known).
source: Thus, all data reuse may be guided by the original or subsequent analyses (a HARKing-like problem where methods are formulated after some results are known [Button, 2019]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Button, 2019.

claim: If adopting Wagenmakers et al., 2012 definition of confirmatory research, it follows that any reuse of open data after publication must be exploratory unless the analysis is preregistered before the data release.
source: Therefore, if adopting this prominent definition of confirmatory research (Wagenmakers et al., 2012), it follows that any reuse of open data after publication must be exploratory unless the analysis is preregistered before the data release.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the definition from Wagenmakers et al., 2012.

claim: Some have said confirmatory analyses may not require preregistrations.
source: Some may find Wagenmakers et al., 2012 definition to be too stringent and instead would rather allow that confirmatory hypotheses can be stated at later dates despite the researchers having some information about the data from previous use. Others have said confirmatory analyses may not require preregistrations (Jebb et al., 2017) and have argued that confirmatory analyses on open data are possible (Weston et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jebb et al., 2017 and Weston et al., 2019.

claim: The temporal displacement of statistical tests can not be considered sufficient reason for creating a new family of statistical tests, as the speed with which a researcher analyzes a dataset is not relevant to the need to control for multiple statistical tests.
source: First, the temporal displacement of statistical tests can not be considered sufficient reason for creating a new family of statistical tests, as the speed with which a researcher analyzes a dataset is not relevant to the need to control for multiple statistical tests.
evidence: This is a logical argument about what should not constitute a new statistical family.

claim: It should not matter who performs the tests; otherwise, one could correct for multiple tests by crowd-sourcing the analysis.
source: Second, it should not matter who performs the tests; otherwise, one could correct for multiple tests by crowd-sourcing the analysis.
evidence: This is a logical argument about what should not constitute a new statistical family.

claim: Statistical tests on open data, which can be run by different people, and at different times, can be part of the same family of tests.
source: Thus if we were to decide that either of the two differentiating properties of sequential tests on open data creates a new family, undesirable correction procedures would be allowable. To prevent this, statistical tests on open data, which can be run by different people, and at different times, can be part of the same family of tests.
evidence: This is a logical conclusion based on the arguments about what should not create new families.

claim: Sequential tests on open data need to consider correction procedures to control the rate of false positives across the family.
source: Since they can be in the same family, sequential tests on open data need to consider correction procedures to control the rate of false positives across the family.
evidence: This is a logical conclusion based on the argument that sequential tests can be part of the same family.

claim: In simulations with 100 sequential statistical tests where the simulated covariance between all variables was 0, there will almost always be at least one false positive when tests are uncorrected.
source: There will almost always be at least one false positive any time one performs 100 sequential analyses with this simulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Uncorrected sequential tests necessarily lead to more false positives.
source: This rate of false positives is dramatically above the desired familywise error rate of at least one false positive in 5% of the simulation's iterations: uncorrected sequential tests necessarily lead to more false positives.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: α-debt can mathematically ensure that the false negative rate is equal to or better than simultaneous correction with Bonferroni.
source: Finally, the method can mathematically ensure that the false negative rate (i.e., type II error) is equal to or better than simultaneous correction with Bonferroni (See Methods).
evidence: This is stated as a mathematical property of the α-debt method.

claim: In α-spending, the sum of all the statistical thresholds for all sequential tests can never exceed the total amount of 'α wealth'.
source: The first has a total amount of 'α wealth', and the sum of all the statistical thresholds for all sequential tests can never exceed this amount (i.e., if the α wealth is 0.05 then the sum of all thresholds on sequential tests must be less than 0.05).
evidence: This is a description of the α-spending method from Foster and Stine, 2008.

claim: In simulations, α-spending limits the probability of there being at least one false positive to less than 0.05.
source: In the simulations, the sequential tests limit the probability of there being at least one false positive to less than 0.05 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: α-investing allows for the significance threshold to increase or decrease as researchers perform additional tests.
source: Finally, α-investing allows for the significance threshold to increase or decrease as researchers perform additional tests.
evidence: This is a description of the α-investing method from Foster and Stine, 2008.

claim: α-investing ensures control of the false discovery rate at an assigned level.
source: α-investing ensures control of the false discovery rate at an assigned level.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the α-investing method from Foster and Stine, 2008.

claim: In simulations, α-investing remains under 0.05 familywise error rate as the sequential tests increase.
source: In the simulations, this method also remains under 0.05 familywise error rate as the sequential tests increase (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The order of the tests is pivotal for sequential correction procedures.
source: The results reveal that the order of the tests is pivotal for sequential correction procedures.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The uncorrected and simultaneous correction procedures do not depend on the sequential order of tests.
source: Unsurprisingly, the uncorrected and simultaneous correction procedures do not depend on the sequential order of tests (Figure 2ABC).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 2ABC.

claim: The sequential correction procedures all increased their true positive rate when the true positives were earlier in the analysis order.
source: The sequential correction procedures all increased their true positive rate (i.e., fewer type II errors) when the true positives were earlier in the analysis order (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The false positive rate and false discovery rate are both very high for the uncorrected procedure.
source: The false positive rate and false discovery rate are both very high for the uncorrected procedure (Figure 2BC).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 2BC.

claim: Using sequentially uncorrected tests on HCP data leads to 30/44 (Bonferroni/FDR) positive findings, compared to a baseline of 2 findings when correcting for all tests simultaneously.
source: Using sequentially uncorrected tests leads to an increase in positive findings (30/44 Bonferroni/FDR), compared to a baseline of 2 findings when correcting for all tests simultaneously (for both Bonferroni and FDR procedures).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the empirical analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The sequentially uncorrected procedures would result in 29/30 (Bonferroni/FDR) publications that claim to identify at least one positive result instead of the simultaneous baseline of two publications, reflecting a 1,400% increase in publications claiming positive results.
source: The sequentially uncorrected procedures would also result in 29/30 (Bonferroni/FDR) publications that claim to identify at least one positive result instead of the simultaneous baseline of two publications (Bonferroni and FDR), reflecting a 1,400% increase in publications claiming positive results.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the empirical analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The other two sequential procedures (α-spending and α-investing) can be more conservative than Bonferroni.
source: At the same time, the other two sequential procedures can be more conservative than Bonferroni.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the empirical analysis results.

claim: The potential of a dataset to identify new statistically significant relationships will decay over time as the number of sequential statistical tests increases when controlling for sequential tests.
source: Broadly, we conclude that the potential of a dataset to identify new statistically significant relationships will decay over time as the number of sequential statistical tests increases when controlling for sequential tests.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the simulations and empirical analysis.

claim: α-spending places restrictions on the initial investigator(s) (and increased type II error rate) which would likely serve as a disincentive for those researchers to share their data.
source: This change could potentially happen with appropriate institutional change, but placing restrictions on the initial investigator(s) (and increased type II error rate) would likely serve as a disincentive for those researchers to share their data.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practical implications of implementing α-spending.

claim: α-spending places incentives to restrict access to open data (violating the open access desideratum) as performing additional tests would lead to a more rapid decay in the ability to detect true positives in a given dataset.
source: It also places incentives to restrict access to open data (violating the open access desideratum) as performing additional tests would lead to a more rapid decay in the ability to detect true positives in a given dataset.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practical implications of implementing α-spending.

claim: Publication bias for positive outcomes would result in statistical thresholds becoming more lenient over time with α-investing, which might lead to even more false positives.
source: Also, publication bias for positive outcomes would result in statistical thresholds becoming more lenient over time with this correction procedure, which might lead to even more false positives (thus violating the no increase in false positives desideratum).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practical implications of implementing α-investing.

claim: α-debt will have little effect on the sharing incentive desideratum as the original study does not need to account for any future sequential tests.
source: However, it will have little effect on the sharing incentive desideratum as the original study does not need to account for any future sequential tests.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practical implications of implementing α-debt.

claim: The open-access desideratum is less likely to be compromised with α-debt as it is less critical to identify the true-positives directly (i.e. it has the lowest type II error rate of the sequential procedures).
source: The open-access desideratum is also less likely to be compromised as it is less critical to identify the true-positives directly (i.e. it has the lowest type II error rate of the sequential procedures).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practical implications of implementing α-debt, supported by simulation results.

claim: While compromising the false positive desideratum, α-debt's false positive rate is a marked improvement compared to sequentially uncorrected tests.
source: Finally, while compromising the false positive desideratum, its false positive rate a marked improvement compared to sequentially uncorrected tests.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation and empirical results comparing α-debt to uncorrected sequential tests.

claim: There is a bias towards the publication of positive findings compared to null findings (file drawer problem).
source: Given the known issues of file drawer problem (Rosenthal, 1979), this is currently problematic to implement (see below).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosenthal, 1979.

claim: Multiple comparisons in Bayesian frameworks are often circumnavigated by partial pooling and regularizing priors.
source: Multiple comparisons in Bayesian frameworks are often circumnavigated by partial pooling and regularizing priors (Gelman et al., 2013; Kruschke and Liddell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gelman et al., 2013 and Kruschke and Liddell, 2017.

claim: Bayesian statistics can suffer from similar problems as NHST if misapplied.
source: While Bayesian statistics can suffer from similar problems as NHST if misapplied (Gigerenzer and Marewski, 2014), it often deals with multiple tests without explicitly correcting for them, and may provide an avenue for sequential correction to be avoided.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gigerenzer and Marewski, 2014.

claim: A well-known problem when creating models to predict on test datasets is overfitting.
source: However, a well-known problem when creating models to predict on test datasets is overfitting.
evidence: This is established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: Reusing test data will occur when sequentially reusing open data.
source: This phenomenon occurs, for example, if a researcher queries the test dataset multiple times. Reusing test data will occur when sequentially reusing open data.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of sequential data reuse in prediction frameworks.

claim: Within machine learning, there have been advances towards having reusable held-out data that can be queried multiple times.
source: Further, within machine learning, there have been advances towards having reusable held-out data that can be queried multiple times (Dwork et al., 2015; Dwork et al., 2017; Rogers et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dwork et al., 2015; Dwork et al., 2017; Rogers et al., 2019.

claim: Cross-validation is not necessarily the best tool in datasets where sample sizes are small.
source: Second, this is ultimately a cross-validation technique which is not necessarily the best tool in datasets where sample sizes are small, (Varoquaux, 2018) which is often the case with open data and thus not a general solution to this problem.
evidence: Supported by citation to Varoquaux, 2018.

claim: In exploratory data analysis (EDA), the primary utility becomes generating hypotheses and testing assumptions of methods.
source: In EDA, the primary utility becomes generating hypotheses and testing assumptions of methods (Donoho, 2017; Jebb et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2020; Tukey, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donoho, 2017; Jebb et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2020; Tukey, 1980.

claim: Accepting that all analyses on open data is EDA would involve less focus on statistical inference — the sequential testing problem disappears.
source: However, accepting that all analyses on open data is EDA would involve less focus on statistical inference — the sequential testing problem disappears.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of treating all open data analyses as exploratory.

claim: Ensuring findings are replicated using independent samples will greatly decrease the false positive rate, since the chance of two identical false positives relationships occurring, even on well-explored datasets, is small.
source: Ensuring findings are replicated using independent samples will greatly decrease the false positive rate, since the chance of two identical false positives relationships occurring, even on well-explored datasets, is small.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the value of replication.

claim: 68 cortical thickness estimates from the 1200 subject release of the HCP dataset were used in the empirical analysis.
source: We used 68 cortical thickness estimates from the 1200 subject release of the HCP dataset (Van Essen et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the data used in the empirical analysis, supported by citation to Van Essen et al., 2012.

claim: 182 behavioral measures ranging from task performance to survey responses were used as dependent variables in the empirical analysis.
source: We then used 182 behavioral measures ranging from task performance to survey responses (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the data used in the empirical analysis.

claim: 182 linear models were fit in which each behavior (dependent variable) was modeled as a function of each of the 68 cortical thickness estimates (independent variables), resulting in a total of 12,376 statistical tests.
source: We fit 182 linear models in which each behavior (dependent variable) was modeled as a function of each of the 68 cortical thickness estimates (independent variables), resulting in a total of 12,376 statistical tests.
evidence: This describes the analysis performed on the HCP data.

claim: All subjects belonging to the HCP dataset gave informed consent.
source: All subjects belonging to this dataset gave informed consent (see Van Essen et al., 2013 for more details).
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Essen et al., 2013.

claim: IRB protocol #31848 approved by the Stanford IRB approves the analysis of shared data.
source: IRB protocol #31848 approved by the Stanford IRB approves the analysis of shared data.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the analysis.
